content: Community-based organization (CBO) workers were frequently identified as a trusted group that could assist individuals in correctly performing self-tests, as they were perceived to be more reliable than other healthcare workers. However, self-testing with a partner or friend was less commonly mentioned as a preferred option. Participants across all sites expressed a strong preference for hepatitis C virus self-testing (HCVST) kits to be provided free of charge. Many believed that if there were any associated costs, even minimal, general populations or at-risk groups would be unlikely to purchase the kits. Concerns were raised about settings where individuals could access HCVST kits but lacked access to confirmatory testing or treatment for hepatitis C. Additionally, there was apprehension that physicians might not accept the results of self-tests. Participants noted that low awareness of hepatitis C in the general population would make it difficult to motivate individuals to purchase HCVST kits. Some participants highlighted that people who inject drugs (PWID) or people who use drugs (PWUD), particularly those concerned about withdrawal symptoms, would prioritize spending their limited resources on drugs rather than on HCVST kits. Homeless individuals were also perceived as highly unlikely to pay for such kits. In India and Indonesia, there were accounts of people living with HIV (PLHIV) in low-income settings, especially women, who had lost all family support and were struggling to survive financially. In India, transgender individuals reported that the economic hardships and unemployment exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic left them prioritizing basic survival over knowing their hepatitis C status, whether through purchasing an HCVST kit or traveling to obtain one for free. Concerns were raised about vulnerable groups, including homeless individuals, transgender women engaged in sex work, people without family support due to their HIV status, and those living in remote and impoverished areas. Many participants emphasized that even if HCVST kits had a cost to cover production, governments should ensure that underserved groups could access them at no charge. However, some participants expressed concerns that if the kits were distributed for free, individuals living in poverty might attempt to resell them to local pharmacies or third parties for income. Despite the general consensus that HCVST kits should be free, some discussions explored what might constitute an acceptable price. Participants noted that if the cost of HCVST kits was similar to other tests, individuals who needed to perform multiple tests might not be able to afford both. For example, a male transgender participant in Brazil stated, If it could just cover production costs, that’d be ideal. A female PWUD participant in Costa Rica remarked, HIV testing was promoted free of cost. Similarly, this can also be made available. If it is given, they may or may not use it, and it could be wasted as well. The assessment highlighted the importance of raising awareness about hepatitis C transmission, diagnosis, and treatment among both the general population and high-risk communities. It was noted that interventions exclusively targeting key populations could exacerbate stigma and discrimination, deterring these groups from seeking HCV care and testing. Efforts to promote HCVST must be paired with full access to care and referral services, including affordable and reliable self-test kits and follow-up treatment. Negative attitudes from healthcare workers (HCWs) toward key populations, as well as paternalistic attitudes toward the general population, were identified as barriers to HCV services. Sensitization, training, and support for HCWs on HCVST and key populations were deemed necessary. Additionally, the diversity within key populations was emphasized, as their experiences, needs, and financial resources vary significantly. Interventions must account for this diversity and ensure that key populations can access services available to the general population. HCVST should be integrated into comprehensive healthcare packages, including linkage to preventive, testing, treatment, and cure services. Offering HCVST as part of routine healthcare services could increase awareness, expand testing coverage, and reduce clinic visits. Integration with other services, such as HIV, STI, TB, antenatal care, and methadone distribution, was also recommended. The development of rapid tests capable of detecting multiple infections, such as HCV, HIV, and STIs, could further support integration efforts. Addressing perceptions of usability and accuracy, particularly for oral fluid-based and fingerprick/whole blood-based HCVST kits, was identified as critical. Education and awareness campaigns through mass media and community groups were recommended to counter misinformation. Disseminating information about registered and quality-assured kits, along with clear messages about their usability and performance, was deemed essential. Regulations and post-market surveillance were also highlighted as necessary to ensure the availability of quality test kits and to minimize the risk of counterfeit products, which could undermine trust in HCVST. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the need to plan HCV service delivery to ensure continuity during health crises. Providing preand post-test information, including brief demonstrations, could address user questions, alleviate potential psychosocial harm, and improve the performance of HCVST kits. Peer support, CBOs, NGOs, and paramedics could play a role in delivering support and messages to key populations through online and in-person services. A system to monitor and mitigate social harms was recommended, which could be adapted to existing country-based systems. Advocacy efforts were deemed necessary to decriminalize key populations and provide non-discriminatory HCV services, including HCVST. A human rights-based approach to HCVST provision was emphasized to ensure that kits are distributed without requiring disclosure, which could increase the risk of stigma and criminalization. Remote areas often lack transportation options, local clinics, laboratories, pharmacies, qualified healthcare providers, or stable access to communication networks. This challenge calls for incorporating HCVST into community-based and rural health systems, such as local health posts, village health authorities, networks of traditional midwives, or partnerships with the private sector. Effective linkage strategies for HCVST should be designed in collaboration with local communities. Priority research gaps include evaluating the acceptability and feasibility of different HCVST service delivery models to reach priority populations and facilitate linkage to confirmatory testing and treatment. Research into social harms related to HCVST, as well as adapting country-level systems to address these concerns, was also deemed important. Developing low-cost, high-sensitivity kits with easily disposable packaging and exploring the potential for multiplex self-tests were identified as areas for further innovation.
